question: When is a runway described as contaminated?

options.text: When more than 10% of it is damp
When any part of it is wet
When over 25% of the surface is contaminated
When there is any standing water at all, even in isolated patches

explanation: A runway is contaminated when more than 25% of the surface area, in patches or not, is covered by standing water over 3 mm, slush or loose snow equal to over 3 mm of water, compacted snow or ice.

question: Above what depth does surface water make a runway contaminated (if it covers enough of the surface)?
explanation: Water more than 3 mm (0.125 in) deep, or slush or loose snow equivalent to 3 mm of water, counts as a contaminant.

question: Which of these is counted as a contaminant even when it is very thin?
explanation: Ice, including wet ice, is listed as a contaminant together with compacted snow, slush, loose snow and deep standing water.

question: What is compacted snow?

options.text: Snow pressed into a solid mass resisting further compression
Snow that has melted and refrozen into a clear sheet of water ice
Loose snow less than 3 mm deep

explanation: Compacted snow has been compressed into a solid mass which resists further compression and holds together or breaks into lumps if picked up.

question: How is a damp runway described?

options.text: Covered by less than 3 mm of standing water over the whole length

explanation: A runway is damp when the surface is not dry but the moisture on it does not make it appear shiny.

question: How is a wet runway described?

options.text: Covered by more than 3 mm of water over half its length

explanation: A wet runway has water less than the contaminated limits, or enough moisture to look reflective, but without significant areas of standing water.

question: A grooved runway kept to give effectively dry braking even when moisture is present is treated as what?
explanation: A dry runway is neither wet nor contaminated, and includes grooved or porous surfaces maintained to keep effectively dry braking action when moist.

question: Above what depth of water, slush or wet snow should a take-off normally not be attempted?
explanation: Take-off should not be attempted with water, slush or wet snow deeper than 15 mm.

question: Above what depth of dry snow should a take-off normally not be attempted?
explanation: The dry snow limit is 60 mm (80 mm for very dry snow); for water, slush or wet snow it is 15 mm.

question: Why is the depth limit higher for dry snow than for slush?

options.text: Dry snow causes less drag and is less dense
Dry snow is always cleared before take-off
Dry snow melts under the tyres

explanation: Slush and water are much denser, so they cause far more impingement and displacement drag than the same depth of dry snow.

question: What causes aquaplaning?

options.text: Low tyre pressure on a dry runway
The tyre rides on a wedge of fluid, losing contact
The brakes lock on dry concrete
The tyres overheat on a dry runway and the rubber starts to melt

explanation: Displaced water forms a bow wave in front of the tyre; above a certain speed the tyre rides up over it and friction falls rapidly.

question: Above what water depth is aquaplaning mainly considered a hazard?
explanation: Aquaplaning must be considered on contaminated runways with about 3 mm or more of water.

question: Which two factors set the aquaplaning speed?

options.text: Tyre pressure and contaminant specific gravity
Aircraft mass and wing area, which set the touchdown speed

explanation: The speed depends on the tyre pressure and the specific gravity of the contaminant: V = 9√(σP) for a rotating tyre.

question: What are the main hazards of aquaplaning?

options.text: Loss of braking and directional control

explanation: Loss of braking action and directional control are the hazards of aquaplaning.

question: Which formula gives the aquaplaning speed in knots for a rotating tyre on water?
explanation: For water (specific gravity 1), V = 9√P knots with P in psi; this is the spin-down speed of a rotating tyre.

question: Which formula gives the aquaplaning speed of a non-rotating tyre at touchdown?
explanation: For a non-rotating tyre (spin-up case at touchdown) the speed is 7.7 times the square root of the pressure in psi.

question: A tyre is inflated to 196 psi. What is its rotating-tyre aquaplaning speed on water?
explanation: √196 = 14; 9 × 14 = 126 kt. The non-rotating value would be 7.7 × 14 ≈ 108 kt.

question: A tyre is inflated to 144 psi. What is the non-rotating aquaplaning speed on water?
explanation: √144 = 12; 7.7 × 12 ≈ 92 kt. The rotating-tyre value would be 9 × 12 = 108 kt.

question: A tyre pressure is given as 10 bar. About how many psi is this?
explanation: 1 bar is about 14.5 psi, so 10 bar ≈ 145 psi.

question: If tyre pressure falls, what happens to the aquaplaning speed?
explanation: The aquaplaning speed is proportional to the square root of tyre pressure, so lower pressure means aquaplaning begins at a lower speed.

question: Why is a non-rotating tyre at touchdown at risk at a lower speed than a rotating one?

options.text: It is not; both are the same
Its aquaplaning speed is lower: 7.7 versus 9 × √P
A non-rotating tyre has higher pressure
A rotating tyre displaces less water than a stationary one

explanation: The spin-up (non-rotating) aquaplaning speed is lower than the spin-down speed, so a landing tyre may fail to spin up on a flooded runway.

question: What can happen to the tyre during prolonged aquaplaning with the wheel locked?

options.text: The tyre gains pressure from the heat and grips the runway better
The tyre inflates and bursts from cold
It can scald, then skid when grip returns

explanation: The locked tyre's energy is dissipated as heat in the contaminant, which may scald the tyre; skidding may follow when aquaplaning breaks down.

question: In the older braking table, which estimated braking action matches a measured coefficient of 0.40 or above?
explanation: In that table: 0.40 and above good (5); 0.39–0.36 medium to good (4); 0.35–0.30 medium (3); 0.29–0.26 medium to poor (2); 0.25 and below poor (1).

question: In the older braking table, which estimated braking action matches a measured coefficient of 0.25 or below?
explanation: 0.25 and below is poor (code 1); 0.29–0.26 is medium to poor (code 2).

question: In the older braking table, a measured coefficient of 0.33 means what braking action?
explanation: 0.35–0.30 is medium (code 3).

question: What does "good" braking action mean on a contaminated runway?

options.text: Braking is better than on a clean dry runway, thanks to the contaminant
As good as a clean, dry runway
No difficulty expected, though not as good as dry

explanation: "Good" is comparative: aeroplanes should have no directional control or braking difficulty, but conditions are not as good as on a clean, dry runway.

question: Which scale is used today to report runway surface condition for each third of the runway?

options.text: A runway condition code from 0 to 6
A letter from A to F

explanation: Current runway condition reports give a runway condition code from 6 (dry) down to 0 for each third, based mainly on contaminant type and depth.

question: On the current runway condition code scale, what does code 6 mean?
explanation: Code 6 is dry; lower codes indicate worse surfaces, down to 0 for the most slippery conditions such as wet ice.

question: Where would a crew find type-specific procedures and performance data for contaminated runways?

options.text: In the operations manual, Part B

explanation: Part B of the operations manual contains type-specific procedures, performance data and wind limits (crosswind, tailwind, gusts) for contaminated runways.

question: What extra limits often apply to take-off and landing on contaminated runways?
explanation: Operations manual data for contaminated runways include wind limits, normally reduced crosswind and tailwind limits.

question: What is a SNOWTAM?

options.text: A report of runway lighting failures caused by snow and ice
A special NOTAM on snow, ice, slush or water
A pilot report of icing in flight

explanation: A SNOWTAM is a special series NOTAM reporting hazardous conditions due to snow, ice, slush, frost or water on the movement area.

question: How long is a SNOWTAM in the current runway-condition format valid at most?
explanation: In the current format a SNOWTAM is valid for at most 8 hours, and a new one is issued whenever there is a significant change. Older formats allowed 24 hours.

question: A runway condition report gives information for which parts of the runway?

options.text: Only the whole runway as one value

explanation: Contaminant type, depth, coverage and condition codes are reported for each third of the runway.

question: Which of these is NOT a contaminant type reported in a runway condition report?
explanation: Reported contaminants include frost, dry snow, wet snow, slush, standing water, ice, compacted snow and frozen ruts; rubber deposits are a maintenance matter.

question: A runway condition report says the cleared runway width or length is less than published. Why does this matter?

options.text: It means the runway is closed until clearing is complete
It has no effect on the crew
Performance must use the reduced distance or width

explanation: When the cleared length or width is less than published, the uncleared part is described, and performance must use the reduced figures.
